property_summary: For any caller and any value sent, calling addToBalance() always increases (or leaves unchanged) that caller's stored userBalance by exactly the sent msg.value (i.e., userBalance(msg.sender) after the call is >= before the call); the mutant that subtracts msg.value can decrease the caller's stored balance, violating this.

For any sender and any payable amount, calling addToBalance increases that sender's userBalance by exactly the sent amount (i.e., userBalance(sender) after call == userBalance(sender) before + msg.value); the mutant removing the require can cause a differing stored balance for some inputs (e.g. when overflow/unchecked logic or other subtle differences occur), so the property will fail on the buggy version for some fuzzed inputs.

For every caller and nonzero sent amount, calling addToBalance() on the correct contract always increases that caller's recorded userBalance by exactly the sent amount (no silent rejection of the increment), while the mutant (which removes the require) can behave differently for some inputs (e.g., by reverting/allowing behavior differences), so the invariant 'after balance == before balance + amount when call succeeds' distinguishes them.

For any actor and amount, if addToBalance succeeds then the contract's total stored balance for that actor equals the contract's previous stored balance for that actor plus the sent amount (i.e., addToBalance never silently fails to update the stored mapping when the call itself succeeds) — the mutant removing the require can make the call succeed but leave balances inconsistent for some inputs.

For any sender and any fuzzed payable amount, if a call to addToBalance succeeds (does not revert) then the contract's recorded userBalance for that sender equals the prior recorded userBalance plus the amount; the mutant (which removes the explicit require) can produce a successful call where this equality does not hold for some fuzzed inputs.

For any caller and any sent value, if addToBalance succeeds then the contract's recorded userBalance for that caller strictly increases by at least the sent amount (i.e., newBalance >= oldBalance + amount); the mutant removing the require can produce executions where this monotonic increase is violated for some inputs.

For any caller and any sent value, calling addToBalance increments userBalance[msg.sender] by the exact sent value (userBalance[msg.sender]_after == userBalance[msg.sender]_before + msg.value); the mutant that checks userBalance[tx.origin] can allow the require to pass or fail based on tx.origin while still updating userBalance[msg.sender], breaking this invariant for some inputs where tx.origin != msg.sender.

For every caller and value, calling addToBalance either always succeeds and increases C.userBalance(msg.sender) by exactly msg.value (reference) — the mutant's require on userBalance[tx.origin] can cause calls from a contract-originated tx to be rejected or to behave differently, so there exist inputs (a contract caller vs tx.origin mismatch) that make the mutant deviate.

For any caller and value, calling addToBalance succeeds when msg.sender is the tx.origin (EOA caller) but may be blocked by the mutant when a contract calls (tx.origin != msg.sender); thus the reference always allows a contract that forwards funds from an EOA-originated tx to increase its own userBalance, while the mutant can reject such calls based on tx.origin, causing a differing post-call userBalance.

For any caller A and any origin O that sends funds through A to C.addToBalance, the reference requires only that C checks A's balance invariants (so A can always add its sent value to userBalance[A] when the require passes), whereas the mutant incorrectly bases the require on userBalance[tx.origin] (O) so a call where tx.origin != msg.sender can be allowed/rejected differently and therefore can change which account's userBalance is updated; the test fuzzes an EOA origin amount and a contract forwarder address to exhibit a case where the reference accepts and updates the forwarder balance but the mutant's tx.origin check blocks it (or vice versa).

For any caller A and any sent amount v, calling addToBalance via a contract forwarder F (where msg.sender == F and tx.origin == EOA) always increments userBalance(F) by v in the reference, whereas the mutant's require tied to userBalance[tx.origin] can block the forwarder and thus cause userBalance(F) to not increase for some (F, EOA, v).

getBalance(u) returns the stored balance for address u (not necessarily the caller) — i.e., for any addr u, c.getBalance(u) equals c.getBalance(u) as viewed by any querier and in particular equals the balance returned when queried with that same address.
After depositing value via addToBalance, querying getBalance for the depositor address returns the deposited amount (i.e., getBalance(depositor) equals the value just sent).
For any caller who just deposited, querying getBalance for some other address u must return a value no greater than the caller's own reported balance (i.e., getBalance(u) ≤ getBalance(msg.sender)).

getBalance(u) always returns the stored balance for the queried address u (i.e., the returned value equals what the contract would send to u), so querying any address u yields that address's own balance, not the caller's.
For any user address u, getBalance(u) returns that user's balance as reflected by deposits/withdrawals (not the contract's own mapping entry).
For any u, getBalance(u) equals getBalance(address(this)) only when u == address(this).
If u != address(this) then c.getBalance(u) != c.getBalance(address(this)).
If u != address(this) then c.getBalance(u) != c.getBalance(address(this)).
For any address u, getBalance(u) equals getBalance(address(this)) only when u == address(this).

For any caller and any address u, getBalance(u) returns that address's stored userBalance entry (userBalance[u]); the mutant that returns userBalance[address(this)] breaks this because for some u (and after deposits) the returned value differs from userBalance[u].

For any caller and any queried address u, getBalance(u) must return the stored userBalance for u (i.e. userBalance[u]); the mutant returns userBalance[address(this)] instead, so after deposits by u (or others) there exist inputs where getBalance(u) differs from that stored balance.

For any depositor addr and any queried address u, calling addToBalance() by depositor then querying getBalance(u) on the reference returns the stored userBalance[u]; the mutant instead always returns userBalance[address(this)] so after a deposit by depositor there exist (depositor,u) pairs where getBalance(u) != userBalance[u].

For every depositor and queried address u, calling addToBalance() by the depositor never changes the invariant that getBalance(u) equals the stored mapping entry userBalance[u] (i.e. getBalance(u) == userBalance[u]); the mutant breaks this because it always returns userBalance[address(this)] so for some depositor and u the two values differ after deposits.
